content: The use of Trecator (ethionamide) as a single agent in the treatment of tuberculosis is not recommended because it leads to the rapid development of drug resistance. It is critical to combine Trecator with one or more companion drugs, chosen based on susceptibility testing results. However, treatment may begin before these results are available if the physician deems it necessary. Ethionamide should always be administered alongside at least one, and sometimes two, other drugs to which the tuberculosis organism is known to be susceptible. Common companion drugs include rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, cycloserine, kanamycin, streptomycin, and isoniazid. The standard warnings, precautions, and dosage guidelines for these companion drugs must also be followed. Patient adherence to the prescribed drug regimen is essential for successful treatment and to prevent the emergence of drug-resistant tuberculosis strains. If drug-resistant tuberculosis develops, consultation with experts in managing such cases is advised. Ethionamide may increase the likelihood of adverse effects from other antituberculous drugs when used in combination. Patients undergoing treatment with Trecator should have regular ophthalmologic evaluations, including ophthalmoscopy, both before starting therapy and periodically during treatment. Patients should be instructed to contact their physician immediately if they experience blurred vision or any loss of vision, whether or not it is accompanied by eye pain. Excessive alcohol consumption should be avoided during treatment, as it has been associated with psychotic reactions. If transaminase levels become elevated, ethionamide and any companion drugs should be temporarily discontinued until the abnormalities resolve. The drugs should then be reintroduced one at a time to identify the agent responsible for hepatotoxicity. Blood glucose levels should also be checked before and periodically during therapy, with diabetic patients being particularly vigilant for signs of hypoglycemia. Thyroid function tests should be performed periodically, as hypothyroidism, with or without goiter, has been reported during ethionamide therapy. Trecator has been shown to temporarily increase serum concentrations of isoniazid. It may also enhance the adverse effects of other antituberculous drugs when used concurrently. Notably, convulsions have been reported when ethionamide is combined with cycloserine, so special caution is required if both drugs are included in the treatment regimen. Excessive alcohol consumption should be avoided due to the risk of psychotic reactions. Animal studies have shown that Trecator has teratogenic potential in rabbits and rats when administered at doses significantly higher than those recommended for humans. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Based on these findings, Trecator should not be used in pregnant women or women who may become pregnant during therapy unless the prescribing physician determines that it is an essential component of the treatment regimen. The effects of Trecator on labor and delivery in pregnant women are unknown. Additionally, there is no information available regarding the excretion of ethionamide in human breast milk. Therefore, Trecator should only be given to nursing mothers if the potential benefits outweigh the risks. Breast-fed infants of mothers taking Trecator should be closely monitored for adverse effects. Pulmonary tuberculosis resistant to primary therapy is rare in neonates, infants, and children, so studies in these populations have been limited. Trecator should not be used in pediatric patients under 12 years of age unless the tuberculosis organism is confirmed to be resistant to primary therapy and the disease is systemically disseminated or poses life-threatening complications.
